metadata.title: Impacts of generative AI on student teachers' task performance and collaborative knowledge construction process in mind mapping-based collaborative environment

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used a quasi-experimental course design with 10 student-teacher groups (5 control, 5 experimental) in a single comprehensive university in central China. The paper does not report the use of any complex survey sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures, and the outcomes are group-level product scores (TPACK gauge) and coded discourse frequencies analyzed via Ordered Network Analysis (ONA). Because the design is an educational intervention with a small, purposively assembled cohort rather than an ILSA-style representative sample, standard ILSA weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) are not applicable here. Consequently, the analysis should be interpreted as internal validity evidence for this course context rather than population-representative inference.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values (PVs) are not applicable because the study does not analyze ILSA cognitive achievement scores; instead, it uses (a) group product ratings on the TPACK gauge and (b) coded collaborative discourse transitions modeled with ONA, plus qualitative interview thematic analysis. Missing-data handling is not reported because the paper does not describe any missingness mechanism or imputation/deletion procedure for the group scores, coded utterances, or interview transcripts. Given the small number of groups and the manual coding/scoring workflow, the authors may have excluded incomplete cases implicitly, but this is not documented.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were student teachers (sophomore/junior) enrolled in an 8-week elective course (“Pedagogical Applications of Information Technology”) at a comprehensive university in central China. All 30 student teachers were first assessed with two instruments (problem-solving ability test adapted from PISA 2005 and a questionnaire on subject pedagogy and technological knowledge), then grouped into 10 groups of 3 based on homogeneity between groups. Five groups were randomly assigned to the control condition (MMCE) and five to the experimental condition (GMMCE) after verifying no significant between-group differences using Kruskal–Wallis tests. The study focuses on two revision rounds (stage 1.2/1.3 for ID and stage 2.2/2.3 for MD) and uses discourse data from synchronous Tencent QQ discussions; utterances were coded at the sentence level using a predefined cognitive/regulative coding framework.

main_findings.dataset_used: Course intervention (2023, Pedagogical Applications of Information Technology) — ID task (instructional design) group product scores (TPACK gauge)
main_findings.target_variable: Task performance: ID product TPACK score
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mann–Whitney U: U = 3.000, z = −1.984, p = 0.047; Experimental (GMMCE) n=5, M=28.8, SD=3.8; Control (MMCE) n=5, M=21.8, SD=5.7
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the course intervention data for the ID task (TPACK gauge group product scores), the study leveraged GAI integration condition alongside pretest problem-solving ability and pedagogy/technology knowledge used for grouping to compare task performance between GMMCE and MMCE groups, finding that GMMCE groups scored significantly higher on ID products (p = 0.047). This indicates that integrating generative AI into mind-mapping-based collaborative scaffolds can improve student teachers’ instructional design quality, though the evidence is limited to a small, single-site cohort and does not establish causal effects beyond this context.

main_findings.dataset_used: Course intervention (2023, Pedagogical Applications of Information Technology) — MD task (multimedia courseware) group product scores (TPACK gauge)
main_findings.target_variable: Task performance: MD product TPACK score
main_findings.performance_metrics: Mann–Whitney U: U = 4.000, z = −1.776, p = 0.076; Experimental (GMMCE) n=5, M=29.4, SD=2.3; Control (MMCE) n=5, M=24.6, SD=4.7
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the course intervention data for the MD task (TPACK gauge group product scores), the study leveraged GAI integration condition alongside pretest problem-solving ability and pedagogy/technology knowledge used for grouping to compare task performance between GMMCE and MMCE groups, finding no statistically significant difference for MD products (p = 0.076). This indicates that generative AI support may be more effective for text/document composition components of collaborative design than for multimedia courseware production, suggesting tool–task fit is critical in instructional design decisions.

main_findings.dataset_used: Course intervention (2023, Pedagogical Applications of Information Technology) — ID task discourse transitions modeled with Ordered Network Analysis (ONA)
main_findings.target_variable: Collaborative knowledge construction process: cognitive vs regulative transition patterns (ONA)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as predictive metrics; qualitative ONA network differences described (e.g., stronger transitions CG→CI and CI→CP in GMMCE during stage 1.2; MMCE shows more regulative-dimension transitions and RI→RG patterns).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the course intervention discourse data for the ID task modeled with Ordered Network Analysis, the study leveraged the GAI integration condition (with grouping based on pretest problem-solving ability and pedagogy/technology knowledge) to characterize collaborative knowledge construction transition patterns across cognitive and regulative dimensions, finding that GMMCE groups showed stronger cognitive-dimension trajectories (e.g., CG→CI and CI→CP) while MMCE groups relied more on regulative transitions (e.g., RI→RG) during early revision. This indicates that generative AI scaffolding can shift collaboration from primarily monitoring/planning toward more cognitive negotiation and consensus-building, which may support deeper collective intelligence formation in collaborative learning.

main_findings.dataset_used: Course intervention (2023, Pedagogical Applications of Information Technology) — MD task discourse transitions modeled with Ordered Network Analysis (ONA)
main_findings.target_variable: Collaborative knowledge construction process: developmental trajectory across task stages (ONA)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported as predictive metrics; qualitative ONA network differences described (e.g., MMCE shows persistent RI→RG and stronger CI→CP with diminished CP→CG; GMMCE shows strong CI→CP, CP→CG, and CG→CI transitions indicating a developmental trajectory).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using the course intervention discourse data for the MD task modeled with Ordered Network Analysis, the study leveraged the GAI integration condition (with grouping based on pretest problem-solving ability and pedagogy/technology knowledge) to compare how collaborative knowledge construction evolves across stages, finding that GMMCE groups maintained a more developmental cognitive trajectory (CI→CP→CG→CI) whereas MMCE groups remained more regulative and showed weaker CP→CG transitions. This indicates that generative AI can help sustain cognitive negotiation across collaborative design phases, but the magnitude may depend on the task’s representational demands (document vs multimedia).

data.outcome_summary: This quasi-experimental study in a 2023 higher-education course (Pedagogical Applications of Information Technology) compared 10 student-teacher groups (n=30 students; 5 control MMCE, 5 experimental GMMCE) using a mind-mapping-based collaborative environment with or without the generative AI tool ERNIE Bot. Task performance was assessed via group product ratings on the TPACK gauge: GMMCE significantly outperformed MMCE on the instructional design (ID) task (M=28.8 vs 21.8; Mann–Whitney U=3.000, p=0.047), while differences on the multimedia courseware (MD) task were not significant (M=29.4 vs 24.6; U=4.000, p=0.076). Collaborative knowledge construction was analyzed with Ordered Network Analysis (ONA) on coded discourse transitions, showing GMMCE shifts toward cognitive negotiation/consensus patterns across stages. Student-teacher interviews indicated higher perceived usefulness for ID revisions than for MD, with limitations tied to ERNIE Bot’s constrained multimodal understanding. No ILSA PVs or survey weights were used; missing-data handling and any weighting strategy are not reported, and the evidence is limited to a single-site, small sample.
